title: Net Climb Stretches
story: A cycling app splits each ride into kilometres and records each one's net height change: +40 for a kilometre that climbs 40 metres, -15 for one that drops 15. This month's challenge awards a badge for every stretch of back-to-back kilometres whose net climb is exactly the height of a famous tower.
Stretches can overlap, and any stretch of one or more kilometres counts. How many badges did your ride earn?
task: Write countStretches(changes, k). Return how many index pairs i ≤ j satisfy changes[i] + changes[i + 1] + ... + changes[j] === k.
Changes and k can be negative or zero. An empty ride returns 0.

examples.explanation: Three stretches add up to 5: kilometres 0 to 1 (2 + 3), 0 to 3 (2 + 3 - 1 + 1) and 3 to 4 (1 + 4). The first two overlap, and both count.
A climb and a matching drop cancel. Kilometres 0 to 1 and 1 to 2 both net 0, so the answer is 2.

hints: Write the running height after each kilometre of [2, 3, -1, 1, 4], starting from 0 before the ride. How can you read the net climb of kilometres 3 to 4 off that list?
The running heights are 0, 2, 5, 4, 5, 9. The climb from kilometre i to j is (height after j) minus (height before i). For kilometres 3 to 4: 9 - 4 = 5.
So a stretch ending here is worth k exactly when some earlier running height equals current - k. The number of stretches ending here is the number of earlier heights with that value.

Walk once, keeping the running height and a map from height → times seen so far, starting with {0: 1} for the start of the ride. At each kilometre, add the change, add count[height - k] to the answer, then record the new height.
bruteForce: For every start i, extend the end j one kilometre at a time with a running total, counting each time it equals k.

That is n(n + 1)/2 stretches, about 200 million for a 20,000 km log. A sliding window cannot help: with descents the total can drop as the window grows, so you never know whether to grow or shrink it.

* @param {number} k  the net climb that earns a badge
* @return {number} how many stretches have a net climb of exactly k

tests.note: empty ride: the empty stretch does not count
all zeros: every one of the 6 stretches counts
only the stretch starting at index 0: needs the starting height 0 in the map
the same running height repeats: needs counts, not a set

walkthrough: Track your running height from the start (a prefix sum). Any stretch's net climb is the height at its end minus the height just before its start. So at each kilometre ask: "how many earlier running heights were exactly k below me?" A map of height → count answers in one step.
Trace [2, 3, -1, 1, 4] with k = 5, starting with seen = {0: 1} (height 0 before the ride):
• The change +2 gives height 2. The map needs -3, which has not been seen, so no badge is added; then 2 is recorded. Badges: 0.
• The change +3 gives height 5. The map needs 0, which was seen once (the start), so kilometres 0 to 1 earn a badge. Badges: 1. Then 5 is recorded.
• The change -1 gives height 4. The map needs -1, which has not been seen, so 4 is only recorded.
• The change +1 gives height 5. The map needs 0, which was seen once, so kilometres 0 to 3 earn a badge. Badges: 2. The height 5 has now been reached twice.
• The change +4 gives height 9. The map needs 4, which was seen once (after kilometre 2), so kilometres 3 to 4 earn a badge. Badges: 3.

Three details matter. Seed the map with {0: 1}, or stretches starting at kilometre 0 are missed. Store counts, not just "seen", because each repeat of a height starts a different stretch. And look up before recording the current height, or with k = 0 you would count an empty stretch.
solution.timeWhy: One pass, with one map lookup and one map update per kilometre.
solution.spaceWhy: The map can hold one entry per distinct running height, up to n + 1 of them.
solution.takeaway: The sum of any contiguous stretch is a difference of two prefix sums. To count stretches with a given sum, walk once with a hash map from prefix sum to how often it has occurred: the Matching Receipts idea applied to running totals.
